name: Orlistat

lead: Orlistat is a capsule that blocks the enzymes that digest dietary fat, so less fat from a meal is absorbed. It is used during cutting phases for gradual fat loss, and some in fat-loss forums described it as a replacement for ephedrine.

It inhibits lipase enzymes in the stomach and pancreas, so part of the fat in a meal leaves in the stool, and very little enters the bloodstream. Trials, including a 1998 European study and a 2-year US trial, found more weight loss than placebo, about 2 to 3 kg extra over 6 to 12 months in one summary. Weight loss is smaller than with newer injectable drugs.

paras: It is taken with meals: 60 mg Alli is sold over the counter, 120 mg Xenical by prescription. It is used alongside a reduced-calorie diet. It works less for people already eating low-fat, and some forum posters report diarrhea and little benefit.

Oily spotting, urgency, gas and loose stools are common, reported in more than 25% of patients in one review, especially after fatty meals. It can reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and the label warns against use after organ transplant or with cyclosporine.

angle.text: Orlistat is used during cutting phases to absorb less dietary fat, so fewer calories reach the body and fat comes off gradually. Trials show a few kilos of weight loss over placebo. Oily stools are a known effect, and it works less for people already eating low-fat.

lead: Orlistat is a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor taken with meals to reduce the amount of dietary fat the body absorbs. It is sold by prescription as Xenical (120 mg capsules) and over the counter as Alli (60 mg capsules), and it acts inside the gut rather than being absorbed into the bloodstream.[1][2][3] For appearance, the route is body fat: blocking roughly 30 percent of the fat in a meal from absorption can widen a calorie deficit alongside a reduced-calorie diet, and pooled trial data put the extra weight loss at about 2 to 3 kg over a year compared with lifestyle change alone.[4]

The drug was developed by Roche from lipstatin, a compound made by the soil bacterium Streptomyces toxytricini, and was approved in the United States in April 1999.[4] The 60 mg Alli was cleared for over-the-counter sale in February 2007 and the EU followed in January 2009.[4] Reviews describe orlistat as one of a handful of drugs available for long-term obesity treatment, with weight loss smaller than that of newer injectable drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.[5][6]

Its characteristic side effects are digestive: oily spotting, urgency, gas and loose stools, reported in more than 25 percent of patients in one review.[5] Wikipedia notes they tend to be worst at the start of treatment and ease over time, and that limiting dietary fat helps control them; the Alli manual frames the effect as a form of aversion therapy that encourages a low-fat diet.[4] In bodybuilding and fat-loss forums such as T Nation, orlistat is discussed as a fat blocker for cutting phases, with some posters reporting diarrhea and little benefit.[7][8][9]

paras: Orlistat is approved as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet for weight loss and weight maintenance in adults, and the prescription version is also approved for some adolescents.[1][3] Its place in appearance culture is as a fat-absorption blocker used during dieting phases.

The Alli label states it is for weight loss in overweight adults aged 18 and older when used with a reduced-calorie, low-fat diet.[3] Grokipedia reports that prescription Xenical is indicated for a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with comorbidities, and for adolescents aged 12 to 16.[1] Studies have also examined its effect on liver fat in obese patients with fatty liver disease, on diabetes prevention and on cholesterol.[10][11][2]

People discuss orlistat as a way to reduce fat absorption while dieting or cutting, with the aim of becoming leaner for the same food intake. Several forum posters ask whether it suits people who already restrict dietary fat, since the drug acts on the fat in a meal.[9][12] Product guidance pairs it with a lower-fat diet, and the digestive effects are linked to fatty meals.[3][4]

A 2026 meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials (5,620 participants) found that combining exercise with medication reduced weight, BMI and body-fat percentage more than exercise alone; the paper included a network-pharmacology analysis of liraglutide and orlistat.[13]

A randomised placebo-controlled trial in obese patients (European Multicentre Orlistat Study Group, 1998) tested weight loss and prevention of regain.[14] A two-year US randomised trial examined weight control and risk-factor reduction.[15] The four-year XENDOS trial enrolled 3,305 obese adults and compared orlistat plus lifestyle change with placebo plus lifestyle change: cumulative incidence of type 2 diabetes was about 9.0 percent on placebo versus 6.2 percent on orlistat, a 37.3 percent relative risk reduction concentrated in people with impaired glucose tolerance, and weight loss was about 5.8 kg versus 3.0 kg.[11] Earlier reviews noted reductions in total and LDL cholesterol over up to two years.[2]

Wikipedia summarises one-year orlistat trials as showing that between about 35 and 55 percent of participants lost at least 5 percent of body mass and roughly 16 to 25 percent lost at least 10 percent, with pooled data pointing to a 2 to 3 kg advantage over lifestyle change alone across a year, and notes that not all mass lost is necessarily fat.[4] The same summary reports that participants regained up to about 35 percent of lost weight after stopping the drug, that orlistat reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes in obese people by an amount comparable to lifestyle change, and that long-term use modestly lowered blood pressure (about 2.5 mmHg systolic and 1.9 mmHg diastolic).[4]

Network meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs place orlistat among the options with smaller average weight loss than semaglutide and tirzepatide.[16][6] A 2023 randomised trial in Asian adults with obesity and fatty liver compared orlistat with a diet.[10] Other registered studies cover uric acid, polycystic ovary syndrome and maintenance after weight loss.[17][18][19]

On safety, a 2013 UK study of 94,695 users found no evidence that orlistat caused liver injury; its authors noted injury incidence was higher around the start of treatment, which may reflect the health changes that led to treatment. An Ontario analysis of 953 patients reported a higher rate of acute kidney injury among users than non-users, and a two-year 1999 trial found breast cancer rates of 0.54 percent on orlistat versus 0.51 percent on placebo.[4]

Reviews report oily fecal spotting, urgency and other gastrointestinal effects in more than 25 percent of patients.[5] The most common are steatorrhea, flatulence, urgent bowel movements and, in some people, fecal incontinence. They are typically most severe at the start of treatment, fade over time and are reduced by limiting dietary fat; Wikipedia says restricting fat to about 15 g per meal helps, and notes that loperamide can help with stool consistency and continence.[4] Grokipedia describes dose dependence.[1]

Because orlistat reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and some nutrients, it can lower their levels, and Grokipedia advises a multivitamin.[4][1] It may reduce blood levels of ciclosporin, so the two should not be given together, and can impair absorption of amiodarone; the UK MHRA has flagged a possible reduction in absorption of antiretroviral HIV medicines.[4] Wikipedia lists contraindications including malabsorption, hypersensitivity, reduced gallbladder function, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and anorexia or bulimia.[4]

The OTC label warns against use after organ transplant, with cyclosporine, in people with food-absorption problems or allergy to ingredients, and advises asking a doctor first with a history of gallbladder problems, kidney stones or pancreatitis.[3] In May 2010 the US FDA approved a revised Xenical label adding a warning about rare cases of severe liver injury.[4]

Orlistat binds covalently to gastric and pancreatic lipases in the gut, preventing them from breaking down dietary triglycerides into absorbable fatty acids, so that a fraction of dietary fat passes into the stool; Wikipedia puts the share at around 30 percent and Grokipedia at 25 to 30 percent.[1][2][4] Systemic absorption is negligible, protein binding is above 99 percent, the elimination half-life is 1 to 2 hours and excretion is fecal.[4]

Laboratory work has also found that orlistat inhibits fatty acid synthase, an enzyme studied in cancer research, and a 2007 crystal structure shows it bound to the human fatty acid synthase thioesterase domain; its poor bioavailability and off-target effects limit that use.[4] Orlistat is the saturated derivative of lipstatin, which developers chose to take forward because it is simpler to make and more stable.[4]

Roche developed orlistat from lipstatin, a natural pancreatic lipase inhibitor produced by Streptomyces toxytricini.[1][4] The European multicentre placebo-controlled trial was published in 1998, and a two-year US trial followed in JAMA.[14][15] The FDA approved prescription Xenical in April 1999.[4]

On 23 January 2006 an FDA advisory panel voted 11 to 3 to recommend over-the-counter sale; Public Citizen opposed it. On 7 February 2007 the agency approved the 60 mg GlaxoSmithKline product Alli, which reached US shelves in June 2007.[4] A 2006 T Nation thread had predicted OTC orlistat might reach mass-market stores.[20] The EMA approved OTC sale in the EU on 21 January 2009, US patent protection expired on 18 June 2009, allowing generics, and Swiss drugstores have sold the 60 mg tablets freely since at least September 2017.[4] A supply shortage in spring 2012, caused by a shortage of one component, raised prices.[4]

Orlistat is sold in two strengths. The 120 mg capsule is prescription-only in the US and elsewhere, while the 60 mg capsule is available over the counter in the US and EU.[4][3] In Australia orlistat has been listed since 2000 as a pharmacist-only medicine, and in 2007 the committee withdrew authorisation for direct-to-consumer advertising of Xenical.[4] In the UK it is pharmacy or prescription-only depending on the product, and generics exist in many countries.[4]
In January 2010 the FDA warned that some counterfeit Alli sold online contained sibutramine instead of orlistat, at at least twice the recommended weight-loss concentration.[4]

Orlistat appears mainly in bodybuilding and fat-loss forums rather than in facial-aesthetics communities. T Nation threads from 2002 to 2017 include questions about combining orlistat with other drugs, its place in contest-preparation stacks, a request for fat-loss help for a girlfriend, and reports of diarrhea.[21][9][22][7][8] A 2006 thread discussed it as a replacement as ephedrine products came under regulatory pressure.[23][20] One poster argued that bodybuilders already follow strict diets and have less use for it.[12]

The practical pattern described is use during a diet or cut, taken with meals, with fat intake lowered to manage digestive effects. Users' reports and the drug's label both tie tolerability to dietary fat.
